children: By Karen Sloan and David Thomas

Simpson Thacher & Bartlett will stop publicly releasing its financial data, according to a person familiar with the decision, making it the third major US law firm to end such disclosures in just over a month.

Kirkland & Ellis, the highest-grossing law firm in the US, in early October said it would no longer report its annual financial results to the American Lawyer — a legal trade publication that releases a closely watched annual ranking of the top 200 law firms by revenue and profits per partner.
New York firm Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison followed suit in late October, informing the American Lawyer that it would stop providing its numbers, the Financial Times reported.

David Gialanella, editor-in-chief of The American Lawyer, said in a statement Thursday that the publication will continue delivering its financial data on law firms regardless of whether some firms end public disclosures.

Other firms are likely to follow, said Vertex Advisors consultant Robert Kamins. He said publicly reported metrics can be misused, misunderstood, or used against a firm to poach its partners. Clients may also view the firms’ figures as boastful, prompting them to question the high rates they charge, he added.
Kirkland stated last month that disclosing the figures "does not provide meaningful value to our clients nor adequately reflect the caliber of our firm’s legal services."

Each of the three firms recently withholding its financial data was among the top 20 by gross revenue on the American Lawyer’s 2025 law firm rankings. At No. 1, Kirkland and Ellis reported gross revenue of more than $10 billion last year and reported to have $11.1 million in average profits per equity partner.

Paul Weiss, ranked No. 13, had a reported $3.3 billion in gross revenue in 2025 with $8.6 million in profits per equity partner. Simpson Thacher was ranked No. 10 with $3.5 billion in gross revenue and $8.5 million profits per equity partner.

Bruce MacEwen, a legal industry consultant at Adam Smith, Esq., said not disclosing financial data to media outlets makes it easier for law firms to institute a so-called "black box" compensation system, meaning lawyers' pay is known only to a select few people.
